* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– [[Ramanujan's constant]]:'' {{math|''e''{{sup|''π''{{sqrt|163}}}}}} = {{val|262537412640768743.99999999999925007259}}... {{OEIS|A060295}}. This number is very close to the integer {{math|640320{{sup|3}} + 744}}. See [[Orders of magnitude (numbers)#10−15|10<sup>−15</sup>]].
* ''Physical culture:'' Highest amount of [[byte]]s lifted by a human is 318,206,335,271,488,635 by [[Hafþór Júlíus Björnsson]].<ref>{{Cite press release|url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20241120839867/en/VDURA-and-Phison-Demonstrate-Show-of-Strength-at-SC24 |title=VDURA and Phison Demonstrate Show of Strength at SC24 - Strongman Hafþór Júlíus Björnsson Lifts Over 282.624 PB of Data |website=www.businesswire.com|access-date=20 November 2024}}</ref>

==10<sup>18</sup>==
[[File:Scrumbled Rubik's Cube.jpg|thumb|≈4.33{{e|19}} [[Rubik's Cube]] positions]]
({{gaps|1|000|000|000|000|000|000}}; 1000<sup>6</sup>; [[Long and short scales|short scale]]: one [[quintillion]]; [[long and short scales|long scale]]: one trillion)

ISO: [[exa-]] (E)
* ''Mathematics:'' The first case of exactly 19 prime numbers between multiples of 100 is 1,468,867,005,116,420,800&nbsp;+&nbsp;''n'',<ref name="A186311"/> for ''n'' = 1, 3, 7, 9, 21, 31, 37, 39, 43, 49, 51, 63, 67, 69, 73, 79, 81, 87, 93.
* ''Mathematics:'' 2<sup>61</sup> − 1 = 2,305,843,009,213,693,951 (≈2.31{{e|18}}) is the ninth Mersenne prime. It was determined to be prime in 1883 by [[Ivan Mikheevich Pervushin]]. This number is sometimes called Pervushin's number.
* ''Mathematics:'' [[Goldbach's conjecture]] has been [[Goldbach's conjecture#Partial results|verified]] for all ''n'' ≤ 4{{e|18}} by a project which computed all prime numbers up to that limit.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Silva |first1=Tomás Oliveira e |title=Goldbach conjecture verification |url=http://www.ieeta.pt/~tos/goldbach.html |access-date=11 April 2021}}</ref>
* ''Computing&nbsp;– Manufacturing:'' An estimated 6{{e|18}} [[transistor]]s were produced worldwide in 2008.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sia-online.org/cs/papers_publications/press_release_detail?pressrelease.id=96|title=60th Birthday of Microelectronics Industry|date=13 December 2007|publisher=Semiconductor Industry Association|access-date=2 November 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081013035645/http://www.sia-online.org/cs/papers_publications/press_release_detail?pressrelease.id=96|archive-date=13 October 2008}}</ref>
* ''Computing&nbsp;– Computational limit of a 64-bit [[Central processing unit|CPU]]'': [[9,223,372,036,854,775,807]] (about 9.22{{e|18}}) is equal to 2<sup>63</sup>−1, and as such is the largest number which can fit into a signed ([[two's complement]]) 64-bit integer on a computer.
* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– [[NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Championship|NCAA basketball tournament]]:'' There are 9,223,372,036,854,775,808 (2<sup>63</sup>) possible ways to enter the [[Bracketology|bracket]].
* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– [[Radix|Bases]]:'' 9,439,829,801,208,141,318 (≈9.44{{e|18}}) is the 10th and (by conjecture) largest number with more than one digit that can be written from [[base 2]] to base 18 using only the digits 0 to 9, meaning the digits for 10 to 17 are not needed in bases greater than 10.<ref>Sequence [http://oeis.org/A131646 A131646] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110901015656/http://oeis.org/A131646 |date=2011-09-01 }} in The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences</ref>
* ''Biology&nbsp;– Insects:'' It has been estimated that the [[insect]] population of the Earth is about 10<sup>19</sup>.<ref>"[https://www.si.edu/Encyclopedia_SI/nmnh/buginfo/bugnos.htm Smithsonian Encyclopedia: Number of Insects] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161228155225/http://www.si.edu/Encyclopedia_SI/nmnh/buginfo/bugnos.htm |date=2016-12-28 }}". Prepared by the Department of Systematic Biology, Entomology Section, [[National Museum of Natural History]], in cooperation with Public Inquiry Services, [[Smithsonian Institution]]. Accessed 27 December 2016. Facts about numbers of insects. Puts the number of individual insects on Earth at about 10 quintillion (10<sup>19</sup>).</ref>
* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– Answer to the [[wheat and chessboard problem]]:'' When doubling the grains of wheat on each successive square of a [[chessboard]], beginning with one grain of wheat on the first square, the final number of grains of wheat on all 64 squares of the chessboard when added up is 2<sup>64</sup>−1 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 (≈1.84{{e|19}}).
* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– Legends:'' The [[Tower of Brahma]] [[legend]] tells about a [[Hindu]] temple containing a large room with three posts, on one of which are 64 [[gold]]en discs, and the object of the [[mathematical game]] is for the [[Brahmins]] in this temple to move all of the discs to another pole so that they are in the same order, never placing a larger disc above a smaller disc, moving only one at a time. Using the simplest algorithm for moving the disks, it would take 2<sup>64</sup>−1 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 (≈1.84{{e|19}}) turns to complete the task (the same number as the wheat and chessboard problem above).<ref>[[Ivan Moscovich]], ''1000 playthinks: puzzles, paradoxes, illusions & games'', Workman Pub., 2001 {{isbn|0-7611-1826-8}}.</ref>
* ''Computing&nbsp;– [[IPv6]]:'' 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 (2<sup>64</sup>; ≈1.84{{e|19}}) possible unique /64 [[subnetwork]]s.
* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– Rubik's Cube:'' There are 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 (≈4.33{{e|19}}) different positions of a 3×3×3 [[Rubik's Cube]].
* ''[[Password strength]]:'' Usage of the 95-character set found on standard computer keyboards for a 10-character [[password]] yields a computationally [[intractability (complexity)|intractable]] 59,873,693,923,837,890,625 (95<sup>10</sup>, approximately 5.99{{e|19}}) permutations.
* ''Internet – YouTube:'' There are 73,786,976,294,838,206,464 (2<sup>66</sup>; ≈7.38{{e|19}}) possible YouTube video URLs.<ref>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |title=Will YouTube Ever Run Out Of Video IDs? |date=21 March 2016 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gocwRvLhDf8 |publisher=Tom Scott}}</ref>
* ''Economics:'' [[Hyperinflation in Zimbabwe]] estimated in February 2009 by some economists at 10 sextillion percent,<ref>{{cite news | title=Scores of Zimbabwe farms 'seized' | url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/africa/7906031.stm | work=BBC | date=23 February 2009 | access-date=14 March 2009 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090301021018/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/africa/7906031.stm | archive-date=1 March 2009 }}</ref> or a factor of 10<sup>20</sup>.
* ''Mathematics:'' 2<sup>68</sup> = 295,147,905,179,352,825,856 is the first [[power of two]] to contain all decimal digits.<ref>{{OEIS|A137214}}</ref>

==10<sup>21</sup>==
[[File:Sudoku Puzzle by L2G-20050714 solution standardized layout.svg|thumb|≈6.7{{e|21}} [[Sudoku]] grids]]
({{gaps|1|000|000|000|000|000|000|000}}; 1000<sup>7</sup>; [[Long and short scales|short scale]]: one [[sextillion]]; [[long and short scales|long scale]]: one thousand trillion, or one [[trilliard]])

ISO: [[zetta-]] (Z)
* ''Geo&nbsp;– Grains of sand:'' All the world's beaches combined have been estimated to hold roughly 10<sup>21</sup> grains of [[sand]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://astronomy.swin.edu.au/~gmackie/billions.html|title=To see the Universe in a Grain of Taranaki Sand|url-status=live|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120630/http://astronomy.swin.edu.au/~gmackie/billions.html|archive-date=2012-06-30}}</ref>
* ''Computing&nbsp;– Manufacturing:'' Intel predicted that there would be 1.2{{e|21}} [[transistor]]s in the world by 2015<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.techradar.com/news/computing-components/processors/intel-predicts-1-200-quintillion-transistors-in-the-world-by-2015-1025851|title=Intel predicts 1,200 quintillion transistors in the world by 2015|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130405010314/http://www.techradar.com/news/computing-components/processors/intel-predicts-1-200-quintillion-transistors-in-the-world-by-2015-1025851|archive-date=2013-04-05}}</ref> and Forbes estimated that 2.9{{e|21}} transistors had been shipped up to 2014.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Handy |first1=Jim |title=How Many Transistors Have Ever Shipped? – Forbes|website=[[Forbes]]|url=http://forbes.com/sites/jimhandy/2014/05/26/how-many-transistors-have-ever-shipped|access-date=1 September 2015|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150630142558/http://www.forbes.com/sites/jimhandy/2014/05/26/how-many-transistors-have-ever-shipped/|archive-date=30 June 2015}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 2<sup>71</sup> = 2,361,183,241,434,822,606,848 is the largest known [[power of two]] not containing the digit 5 in its decimal representation.<ref>{{OEIS|A035060}}</ref> The same is true for the digit 7.<ref>{{OEIS|A035062}}</ref>
* ''Chemistry:'' There are about 5{{e|21}} atoms in a drop of water.<ref>{{cite web |last=Helmenstine|first=Anne|date=2019-08-27|title=Calculating the Number of Atoms and Molecules in a Drop of Water|url=https://www.thoughtco.com/atoms-in-a-drop-of-water-609425|website=ThoughtCo.|publisher=Anne Marie Helmenstine, Ph.D.|access-date=2025-05-15}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– Sudoku:'' There are 6,670,903,752,021,072,936,960 (≈6.7{{e|21}}) possible (unique) 9×9 [[Sudoku]] grids.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.afjarvis.staff.shef.ac.uk/sudoku/bertram.html|title=Sudoku enumeration|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061006193945/http://www.afjarvis.staff.shef.ac.uk/sudoku/bertram.html|archive-date=2006-10-06}}</ref>
* ''Computing:'' 10,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 (10<sup>22</sup>)&nbsp;– number up to which all powers of 10 can be exactly represented in IEEE [[double precision floating-point format]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Regan|first=Rick|date=2011-08-11|title=Why Powers of Ten Up to 10<sup>22</sup> Are Exact As Doubles|url=https://www.exploringbinary.com/why-powers-of-ten-up-to-10-to-the-22-are-exact-as-doubles/|website=Exploring Binary|publisher=Rick Regan|access-date=2025-05-15}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' The smallest instance of exactly 20 prime numbers between multiples of 100 is 20,386,095,164,137,273,086,400&nbsp;+&nbsp;''n'',<ref name="A186311"/> for ''n'' = 1, 3, 7, 9, 13, 19, 21, 31, 33, 37, 49, 57, 63, 73, 79, 87, 91, 93, 97, 99.
* ''Mathematics:'' 5<sup>32</sup> = 23,283,064,365,386,962,890,625 is the largest known power of five not containing a pair of consecutive equal digits.<ref>{{OEIS|A050726}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 24,153,319,581,254,312,065,344 is the sixth and largest known [[taxicab number]].
* ''Astronomy&nbsp;– Stars:'' 70 sextillion = 7{{e|22}}, the estimated number of [[star]]s within range of [[telescope]]s (as of 2003).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://msowww.anu.edu.au/news/media_releases/media_release_030717.php |title=Star count: ANU astronomer makes best yet |date=17 July 2003 |publisher=The Australian National University |access-date=2 November 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050724115154/http://msowww.anu.edu.au/news/media_releases/media_release_030717.php |archive-date=July 24, 2005 }}</ref>
* ''Astronomy&nbsp;– Stars:'' in the range of 10<sup>23</sup> to 10<sup>24</sup> stars in the [[observable universe]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Astronomers count the stars|publisher=BBC News|date=July 22, 2003|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/3085885.stm|access-date=2006-07-18|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060813153925/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/3085885.stm|archive-date=August 13, 2006}}
[https://www.npr.org/blogs/thetwo-way/2010/12/01/131730552/ "trillions-of-earths-could-be-orbiting-300-sextillion-stars"]
{{cite journal|last = van Dokkum|first =Pieter G.|author2=Charlie Conroy|title = A substantial population of low-mass stars in luminous elliptical galaxies |journal = Nature|volume = 468|issue = 7326|pages = 940–942|date = 2010|pmid = 21124316|doi = 10.1038/nature09578 |bibcode = 2010Natur.468..940V |arxiv = 1009.5992 |s2cid =205222998}}
[http://www.universetoday.com/24328/how-many-stars/ "How many stars?"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130122232925/http://www.universetoday.com/24328/how-many-stars/ |date=2013-01-22 }}; see [[mass of the observable universe]]</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 146,361,946,186,458,562,560,000 (≈1.5{{e|23}}) is the fifth and largest known [[unitary perfect number]].
* ''Mathematics:'' 357,686,312,646,216,567,629,137 (≈3.6{{e|23}}) is the largest [[left-truncatable prime]].
[[File:Avogadro number cube visualisation.svg|thumb|upright|Visualisation of a [[Mole (unit)|mole]] of 1 mm<sup>3</sup> cubes arranged into a cube with {{convert|84.4|km|mi|abbr=on}} sides, overlaid on maps of [[South East England]] and [[London]] (top), and [[Long Island]] and [[New York City]] (bottom)]]
* ''Mathematics:'' 2<sup>78</sup> = 302,231,454,903,657,293,676,544 is the largest known [[power of two]] not containing the digit 8 in its decimal representation.<ref>{{OEIS|A035063}}</ref>
* ''Chemistry&nbsp;– Physics:'' The [[Avogadro constant]] ({{val|6.02214076|e=23}}) is the number of constituents (e.g. atoms or molecules) in one [[mole (unit)|mole]] of a substance, defined for convenience as expressing the order of magnitude separating the molecular from the [[macroscopic scale]].

* ''Mathematics:'' 2<sup>86</sup> = 77,371,252,455,336,267,181,195,264 is the largest known [[power of two]] not containing the digit '0' in its decimal representation.<ref>{{OEIS|A007377}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 2<sup>89</sup> − 1 = 618,970,019,642,690,137,449,562,111 (≈6.19{{e|26}}) is the tenth [[Mersenne prime]]. See [[List of Mersenne primes and perfect numbers]].

({{gaps|1|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000}}; 1000<sup>9</sup>; [[Long and short scales|short scale]]: one [[octillion]]; [[long and short scales|long scale]]: one thousand quadrillion, or one quadrilliard)

* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– Poker:'' the number of unique combinations of hands and shared cards in a 10-player game of [[Texas hold 'em]] is approximately 2.117{{e|28}}.

({{gaps|1|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000}}; 1000<sup>11</sup>; [[Long and short scales|short scale]]: one [[decillion]]; [[long and short scales|long scale]]: one thousand quintillion, or one quintilliard)
* ''Computing:'' 10,384,593,717,069,655,257,060,992,658,440,192 (2<sup>113</sup>)&nbsp;– number until which all integer values can exactly be represented in IEEE [[quadruple-precision floating-point format]].<ref>Significand precision is 113 bits. 10,384,593,717,069,655,257,060,992,658,440,192 can be represented with 1 bit of precision. ({{gaps|1|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000}}; 1000<sup>12</sup>; [[Long and short scales|short scale]]: one [[undecillion]]; [[long and short scales|long scale]]: one [[sextillion]])
* ''Biology:'' The total number of [[DNA]] base pairs on Earth is estimated at 5.0{{e|37}}.<ref name="NYT-20150718-rn">{{cite news | vauthors = Nuwer R |author-link=Rachel Nuwer |date=18 July 2015 |title=Counting All the DNA on Earth |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/07/21/science/counting-all-the-dna-on-earth.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220101/https://www.nytimes.com/2015/07/21/science/counting-all-the-dna-on-earth.html |archive-date=2022-01-01 |url-access=limited |work=The New York Times |location=New York |issn=0362-4331 |access-date=2025-03-28}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

* ''Computing:'' 2<sup>128</sup> = 340,282,366,920,938,463,463,374,607,431,768,211,456 (≈3.40282367{{e|38}}), the theoretical maximum number of Internet addresses that can be allocated under the [[IPv6]] addressing system, the total number of different [[Universally Unique Identifier]]s (UUIDs) that can be generated, and the total number of different possible keys in the [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]] 128-bit [[key space (cryptography)|key space]] (symmetric cipher).

({{gaps|1|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000}}; 1000<sup>13</sup>; [[Long and short scales|short scale]]: one [[duodecillion]]; [[long and short scales|long scale]]: one thousand sextillion, or one sextilliard)
* ''Cosmology:'' The [[Eddington–Dirac number]] is roughly 10<sup>40</sup>.

Cosmological parameters (See Table 4 on page 31 of pfd).|url=https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/planck-2015-results(491d214e-7255-415e-97b5-96d8ae621eaa).html|journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics|volume=594|page=A13|arxiv=1502.01589|bibcode=2016A&A...594A..13P|doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201525830|doi-access=free|s2cid=119262962}}</ref>

==10<sup>63</sup> to 10<sup>100</sup>==
({{gaps|1|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000}}; 1000<sup>21</sup>; [[Long and short scales|short scale]]: one [[vigintillion]]; [[long and short scales|long scale]]: one thousand [[decillion]], or one [[decilliard]])
* ''Cosmology:'' 1{{e|63}} is [[Archimedes]]' estimate in ''[[The Sand Reckoner]]'' of the total number of grains of [[sand]] that could fit into the entire [[cosmos]], the diameter of which he estimated in [[stadion (unit)|stadia]] to be what we call 2 [[light-year]]s.
* ''Mathematics:'' 3<sup>133</sup> = 2,865,014,852,390,475,710,679,572,105,323,242,035,759,805,416,923,029,389,510,561,523 is the largest known [[power of three]] not containing a pair of consecutive equal digits.<ref>{{OEIS|A050724}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– Cards:'' 52[[factorial|!]] = 80,658,175,170,943,878,571,660,636,856,403,766,975,289,505,440,883,277,824,000,000,000,000 (≈8.07{{e|67}})&nbsp;– the number of ways to order the [[Playing card|cards]] in a 52-card deck.
* ''Mathematics:'' There are 100,669,616,553,523,347,122,516,032,313,645,505,168,688,116,411,019,768,627,200,000,000,000 (≈1.01×10<sup>68</sup>) possible combinations for the [[Megaminx]].
* ''Computing:'' 2<sup>237</sup> = 220,855,883,097,298,041,197,912,187,592,864,814,478,435,487,109,452,369,765,200,775,161,577,472 (≈2.21×10<sup>71</sup>)&nbsp;– number until which all integer values can exactly be represented in IEEE [[octuple-precision floating-point format|octuple precision floating-point format]].<ref>Significand precision is 237 bits. 220,855,883,097,298,041,197,912,187,592,864,814,478,435,487,109,452,369,765,200,775,161,577,472 can be represented with 1 bit of precision. The previous integer requires 237 bits of precision, but the next one would require 238.</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 1,808,422,353,177,349,564,546,512,035,512,530,001,279,481,259,854,248,860,454,348,989,451,026,887 (≈1.81{{e|72}})&nbsp;– The largest known [[prime factor]] found by [[Lenstra elliptic-curve factorization]] (LECF) {{As of|2010|lc=on}}.<ref>[[Paul Zimmermann (mathematician)|Paul Zimmermann]], "[http://www.loria.fr/~zimmerma/records/top50.html 50 largest factors found by ECM] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090220133814/http://www.loria.fr/~zimmerma/records/top50.html |date=2009-02-20 }}".</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' There are 282,870,942,277,741,856,536,180,333,107,150,328,293,127,731,985,672,134,721,536,000,000,000,000,000 (≈2.83{{e|74}}) possible permutations for the [[Professor's Cube]] (5×5×5 Rubik's Cube).
* ''Cryptography:'' 2<sup>256</sup> =  115,792,089,237,316,195,423,570,985,008,687,907,853,269,984,665,640,564,039,457,584,007,913,129,639,936 (≈1.15792089{{e|77}}), the total number of different possible keys in the [[Advanced Encryption Standard]] (AES) 256-bit [[key space (cryptography)|key space]] (symmetric cipher).
* ''Cosmology:'' Various sources estimate the total number of [[fundamental particle]]s in the [[observable universe]] to be within the range of 10<sup>80</sup> to 10<sup>85</sup>.<ref>Matthew Champion, [http://www.madsci.org/posts/archives/oct98/905633072.As.r.html "Re: How many atoms make up the universe?"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120511190951/http://www.madsci.org/posts/archives/oct98/905633072.As.r.html |date=2012-05-11 }}, 1998</ref><ref name="nasawmap">[http://map.gsfc.nasa.gov/universe/uni_matter.html WMAP- Content of the Universe] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160726014944/http://map.gsfc.nasa.gov/universe/uni_matter.html |date=2016-07-26 }}. Map.gsfc.nasa.gov (2010-04-16). Retrieved on 2011-05-01.</ref> However, these estimates are generally regarded as guesswork. (Compare the [[Eddington number]], the estimated total number of protons in the observable universe.)
* ''Computing:'' 9.999 999{{e|96}} is equal to the largest value that can be represented in the IEEE [[decimal32 floating-point format]].
* ''Computing:'' 69! (roughly 1.7112245{{e|98}}), is the largest [[factorial]] value that can be represented on a calculator with two digits for powers of ten without overflow.
* ''Mathematics:'' One [[googol]], 1{{e|100}}, 1 followed by one hundred zeros, or 10,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000.

==10<sup>100</sup> (one googol) to 10<sup>1000</sup>==

[[File:FloorGoban.JPG|thumb|≈2.08{{e|170}} legal [[Go (game)|Go]] positions]]

{{see also|googol}}
({{gaps|10|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000|000}}; [[Long and short scales|short scale]]: ten duotrigintillion; [[long and short scales|long scale]]: ten thousand [[sexdecillion]], or ten sexdecillard)<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://bmanolov.free.fr/numbers_names.php|title=Names of large and small numbers|publisher=Miscellaneous pages by Borislav Manolov|website=bmanolov.free.fr|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160930211121/http://bmanolov.free.fr/numbers_names.php|archive-date=2016-09-30}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' The first instance of two consecutive 4's in [[Gijswijt's sequence]] begins at index 255 895 648 634 818 208 370 064 452 304 769 558 261 700 170 817 472 823 398 081 655 524 438 021 806 620 809 813 295 008 281 436 789 493 636 144 ≈ {{val|2.5590e107}}.<ref name=gijswijt>{{cite arXiv |eprint=2209.04657 |first=Levi |last=van de Pol |title=The first occurrence of a number in Gijswijt's sequence|date=2022 |class=math.CO }}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' There are <math>\frac{8! \times 3^7 \times 24!^6}{24^{25}}</math> ≃ {{val|1.5715e116}} distinguishable permutations of the [[V-Cube 6]] (6×6×6 Rubik's Cube).
* ''Chess:'' [[Shannon number]], 10<sup>120</sup>, a lower bound of the [[game-tree complexity]] of chess.
* ''Physics:'' 10<sup>120</sup>, [[Cosmological constant problem|discrepancy]] between the observed value of the [[cosmological constant]] and a naive estimate based on [[Quantum Field Theory]] and the [[Planck energy]].
* ''Physics:'' 5.9{{e|121}}, ratio of the mass-energy in the [[observable universe]] to the energy of a photon with a wavelength the size of the [[observable universe]].
* ''History&nbsp;– Religion:'' [[Asaṃkhyeya]] is a [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] name for the number 10<sup>140</sup>. It is listed in the [[Avatamsaka Sutra]] and metaphorically means "innumerable" in the [[Sanskrit]] language of [[History of India|ancient India]].
* ''Xiangqi:'' 10<sup>150</sup>, an estimation of the game-tree complexity of [[xiangqi]].
* ''Mathematics:'' [[Primorial|347#]] × 23# × 11 × 7 × 5<sup>2</sup> × 3<sup>4</sup> × 2<sup>8</sup> ≈ {{val|6.6737e153}} is the largest number that is both [[Superabundant number|superabundant]] and [[Highly composite number|highly composite]].<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A166981|Superabundant numbers that are highly composite}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 2<sup>521</sup> − 1 ≈ {{val|8.8648e156}} is the largest known prime which is simultaneously a [[Mersenne prime]] and [[Woodall prime]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Prime Curios! 68647...57151 (157-digits)|url=https://t5k.org/curios/page.php?number_id=3264|access-date=2025-04-03|website=t5k.org|language=en}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' There are <math>\frac{8! \times 3^7 \times 12! \times 2^{10} \times 24!^8}{24^{36}}</math> ≈ {{val|1.9501e160}} distinguishable permutations of the [[V-Cube 7]] (7×7×7 Rubik's Cube).
* ''Go:'' There are 208 168 199 381 979 984 699 478 633 344 862 770 286 522 453 884 530 548 425 639 456 820 927 419 612 738 015 378 525 648 451 698 519 643 907 259 916 015 628 128 546 089 888 314 427 129 715 319 317 557 736 620 397 247 064 840 935 (≈2.08{{e|170}}) [[Go and mathematics#Legal positions|legal positions in the game of Go]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Counting Legal Positions in Go |url=https://tromp.github.io/go/legal.html |website=tromp.github.io |access-date=26 February 2026}}</ref>
* ''Economics:'' The annualized rate of the [[Hungarian pengő#Hyperinflation|hyperinflation in Hungary]] in 1946 was estimated to be 2.9{{e|177}}%.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hanke |first1=Steve |last2=Krus |first2=Nicholas |title=Hyperinflation Table |url=https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/88/The_Hanke_Krus_Hyperinflation_Table.pdf |access-date=26 March 2021}}</ref> It was the most extreme case of [[hyperinflation]] ever recorded.
* ''Board games:'' 3.457{{e|181}}, number of ways to arrange the tiles in [[English-language Scrabble|English ''Scrabble'']] on a standard 15-by-15 ''Scrabble'' board.
* ''Physics:'' 8{{e|184}}, approximate number of [[Planck volume]]s in the [[observable universe]].
* ''Mathematics:'' There are <math>\frac{60!^2 \times 30! \times 2^{29}}{8}</math> ≈ {{val|1.2325e204}} distinguishable permutations of the [[Tuttminx]].
* ''Mathematics:'' There are <math>\frac{8! \times 3^7 \times 24!^{12}}{24^{55}}</math> ≈ {{val|3.5174e217}} distinguishable permutations of the [[V-Cube 8]] (8×8×8 Rubik's Cube).
* ''Shogi:'' 10<sup>226</sup>, an estimation of the game-tree complexity of [[shogi]].
* ''Physics:'' 7{{e|245}}, approximate spacetime volume of the history of the observable universe in [[Planck units]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.richardeldridge.com/impossible.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201003195654/http://www.richardeldridge.com/impossible.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=October 3, 2020|title=Richard Eldridge}}</ref>
* ''Computing:'' 170! (roughly 7.2574156{{e|306}}), is the largest [[factorial]] value that can be represented in the IEEE [[double precision floating-point format]].
* ''Computing:'' 2<sup>1024</sup> × (1 - 2<sup>−53</sup>) ≈ {{val|1.797693134862316e308}} is the largest value that can be represented in the IEEE [[double precision floating-point format]].
* ''Mathematics:'' 1.397162914{{e|316}} is an estimate of a value of <math>x</math> for which <math>\operatorname{li}(x) < \pi(x)</math> (known as [[Skewes's number]]) given by Stoll & Demichel (2011).<ref>{{citation|first1=Douglas|last1=Stoll| first2=Patrick|last2= Demichel|title= The impact of <math>\zeta(s)</math> complex zeros on <math>\pi(x)</math> for <math>x < 10^{10^{13}}</math>|year=2011|journal=[[Mathematics of Computation]]|volume=80|issue=276|pages=2381–2394|mr=2813366|doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-2011-02477-4|doi-access=free}}</ref> A proved upper bound of exp(727.951346802) < 1.397182091{{e|316}} (without assuming the [[Riemann hypothesis]]) or exp(727.951338612) < 1.397170648{{e|316}} (assuming RH) is given by Zegowitz (2010).<ref>{{citation|last=Zegowitz|first=Stefanie|title=On the positive region of <math>\pi(x)-\operatorname{li}(x)</math>|year=2010|url=http://eprints.ma.man.ac.uk/1547/|publisher=Manchester Institute for Mathematical Sciences, School of Mathematics, University of Manchester|series=Master's thesis|type=masters }}</ref>
* ''Computing:'' (10 – 10<sup>−15</sup>){{e|384}} is equal to the largest value that can be represented in the IEEE [[decimal64 floating-point format]].
* ''Mathematics:'' 997# × 31# × 7 × 5<sup>2</sup> × 3<sup>4</sup> × 2<sup>7</sup> ≈ {{val|7.1289e432}} is the [[least common multiple]] of every integer from 1 to 1000.
* ''Physics:'' The number of distinct [[compactification (physics)|compactified]] vacua in [[type IIB string theory]] is estimated at around 10<sup>500</sup>.<ref name="Taylor & Wang 2015">{{cite journal |last1=Taylor |first1=Washington |last2=Wang |first2=Yi-Nan |title=The F-theory geometry with most flux vacua |journal=Journal of High Energy Physics |date=December 2015 |volume=2015 |issue=12 |pages=1–21 |doi=10.1007/JHEP12(2015)164|arxiv=1511.03209 }}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 2063# × 73# × 23# × 11 × 7<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>7</sup> × 2<sup>12</sup> ≈ {{val|4.5794e917}} is the smallest positive integer to exceed a googol divisors.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Highly composite numbers |url=https://wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/highly.html |access-date=2025-11-01 |website=wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de}}</ref> It is the 24,067th [[highly composite number]], and its number of divisors is 2<sup>303</sup> × 3<sup>13</sup> × 5 × 7 × 11 ≈ {{val|1.0002e100}}.

==10<sup>1000</sup> to 10<sup>1,000,000</sup>==
* ''Mathematics:'' 4713 × 2<sup>4713</sup> + 1  ≈ 2.68{{e|1422}} is the third [[Cullen prime]].
* ''Mathematics:'' There are approximately 1.869{{e|4099}} distinguishable permutations of the world's largest [[Rubik's Cube]] (33×33×33).
* ''Computing:'' 2<sup>16384</sup> × (1 − 2<sup>−64</sup>) ≈ {{val|1.18973149535723176505e4932}} is the largest value that can be represented in the IEEE 80-bit x86 [[extended precision]] floating-point format.
* ''Computing:'' 2<sup>16384</sup> × (1 − 2<sup>−113</sup>) ≈ {{val|1.1897314953572317650857593266280070e4932}} is the largest value that can be represented in the IEEE [[quadruple-precision floating-point format]].
* ''Computing:'' (10 – 10<sup>−33</sup>){{e|6144}} is the largest value that can be represented in the IEEE [[decimal128 floating-point format]].
* ''Computing:'' 10<sup>10,000</sup> − 1 is equal to the largest value that can be represented in [[Windows Phone]]'s calculator.
* ''Mathematics:'' ''F''<sub>201107</sub> is a 42,029-digit [[Fibonacci prime]]; the largest known certain Fibonacci prime {{as of|2023|09|lc=on}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Top Twenty: Fibonacci Number |url=https://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=39 |website=primes.utm.edu |access-date=25 March 2025}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' ''L''<sub>202667</sub> is a 42,355-digit [[Lucas prime]]; the largest confirmed Lucas prime {{as of|2023|11|lc=on}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Top Twenty: Lucas Number |url=https://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=48 |website=primes.utm.edu |access-date=2 April 2025}}</ref>
* ''Computing:'' 10<sup>75257</sup> is equal to the largest power of ten that can be represented in [[Android (Google)|Android's Google calculator.]]
* ''Computing:'' 2<sup>250,000</sup> is equal to the largest odd power of two that can be represented in [[Android google|Android Google's calculator]].
* ''Computing:'' 2<sup>262144</sup> × (1 − 2<sup>−237</sup>) ≈ {{val|1.61132571748576047361957211845200501064402387454966951747637125049607183e78913}} is the largest value that can be represented in the IEEE [[octuple-precision floating-point format]].
* ''Mathematics:'' (10<sup>109297</sup> − 1)/9, with 109,297 digits, is the largest proven [[repunit prime]] in base 10 {{As of|2025|5|lc=on}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=PrimePage Primes: Repunit |url=https://t5k.org/top20/page.php?id=57 |website=t5k.org |access-date=25 February 2026 |language=en}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' approximately 7.76 × 10<sup>206,544</sup> cattle in the smallest herd which satisfies the conditions of [[Archimedes's cattle problem]].
* ''Physics:'' The number of distinct compactified vacua in the string theory landscape is estimated in [[F-theory]] at around 10<sup>272,000</sup>.<ref name="Taylor & Wang 2015"/>
* ''Mathematics:'' 2,618,163,402,417 × 2<sup>1,290,000</sup> − 1 is a 388,342-digit [[Sophie Germain prime]]; the largest known {{As of|2023|4|lc=on}}.<ref>Chris Caldwell, [http://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=2 The Top Twenty: Sophie Germain (p)] at The [[Prime Pages]].</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 2,996,863,034,895  ×  2<sup>1,290,000</sup> ± 1 are 388,342-digit [[twin prime]]s; the largest known {{As of|2023|04|lc=on}}.<ref>Chris Caldwell, [https://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=1 The Top Twenty: Twin] at The [[Prime Pages]].</ref>

==10<sup>1,000,000</sup> to 10<sup>10<sup>100</sup></sup> (one googolplex)==

{{see also|googolplex}}
[[File:Digits in largest prime found as a function of time.svg|thumb|Digit growth in the [[largest known prime]]]]

* ''Mathematics:'' ''L''<sub>5466311</sub> is a 1,142,392-digit [[Lucas prime|Lucas probable prime]]; the largest known {{as of|2022|08|lc=on}}.<ref>{{cite web |title=Henri & Renaud Lifchitz's PRP Top - Search by form |url=http://www.primenumbers.net/prptop/searchform.php?form=L%28n%29&action=Search |website=www.primenumbers.net |access-date=2 April 2025}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– Literature:'' [[Jorge Luis Borges]]' [[Library of Babel]] contains at least 25<sup>1,312,000</sup> ≈ 1.956 × 10<sup>1,834,097</sup> books (this is a lower bound).<ref>From the third paragraph of the story: "Each book contains 410 pages; each page, 40 lines; each line, about 80 black letters." That makes 410 &times; 40 &times; 80 = 1,312,000 characters.  The fifth paragraph tells us that "there are 25 orthographic symbols" including spaces and punctuation.  The magnitude of the resulting number is found by taking logarithms. However, this calculation only gives a lower bound on the number of books as it does not take into account variations in the titles&nbsp;– the narrator does not specify a limit on the number of characters on the spine.  For further discussion of this, see Bloch, William Goldbloom. ''[[The Unimaginable Mathematics of Borges' Library of Babel]]''. Oxford University Press: Oxford, 2008.</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 4 × 72<sup>1,119,849</sup> − 1 is the smallest prime of the form 4 × 72<sup>''n''</sup> − 1.<ref>Gary Barnes, [http://www.noprimeleftbehind.net/crus/Riesel-conjectures.htm Riesel conjectures and proofs] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412022834/http://www.noprimeleftbehind.net/crus/Riesel-conjectures.htm|date=2021-04-12}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 2<sup>6,972,593</sup> − 1 is a 2,098,960-digit [[Mersenne prime]]; the 38th Mersenne prime and the last Mersenne prime discovered in the 20th century.<ref name="mersenneprime" />
* ''Mathematics:'' ''F''<sub>10367321</sub> is a 2,166,642-digit probable Fibonacci prime; the largest known {{as of|2024|07|lc=on}}.<ref name="prptop">[http://www.primenumbers.net/prptop/searchform.php?form=F%28n%29&action=Search PRP Top Records, Search for : F(n)]. Retrieved 2025-03-25.</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 10<sup>2,718,281</sup> − 5 &times; 10<sup>1,631,138</sup> – 5 &times; 10<sup>1,087,142</sup> − 1 is a 2,718,281-digit [[palindromic prime]], the largest known {{As of|2025|09|lc=on}}.<ref>Chris Caldwell, [http://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=53 The Top Twenty: Palindrome] at The [[Prime Pages]].</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 632,760!&nbsp;- 1 is a 3,395,992-digit [[factorial prime]]; the largest known {{As of|2025|09|lc=on}}.<ref>Chris Caldwell, [http://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=30 The Top Twenty: Factorial primes] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130410122813/http://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=30 |date=2013-04-10 }} at The [[Prime Pages]].</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 9,562,633# + 1 is a 4,151,498-digit [[primorial prime]]; the largest known {{As of|2025|09|lc=on}}.<ref>Chris Caldwell, [http://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=5 The Top Twenty: Primorial] at The [[Prime Pages]].</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' (2<sup>15,135,397</sup> + 1)/3 is a 4,556,209-digit [[Wagstaff prime|Wagstaff probable prime]], the largest known {{as of|2021|06|lc=on}}.
* ''Mathematics:'' 81 × 2<sup>20,498,148</sup> + 1 is a 6,170,560-digit [[Pierpont prime]], the largest known {{as of|2023|lc=on}}.<ref>{{citation|url=http://primes.utm.edu/primes/lists/short.txt|title=The largest known primes|first=Chris|last=Caldwell|website=The [[Prime Pages]]|access-date=7 April 2025|archive-date=9 November 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109191109/http://primes.utm.edu/primes/lists/short.txt}}; {{citation|url=https://primes.utm.edu/primes/page.php?id=136165|title=The Prime Database: 81*2^20498148+1|website=The [[Prime Pages]]|access-date=7 April 2025}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' (10<sup>8,177,207</sup> − 1)/9 is an 8,177,207-digit [[probable prime]], the largest known {{as of|2021|5|8|lc=on}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.primenumbers.net/prptop/prptop.php|title=Henri & Renaud Lifchitz's PRP Top records|website=www.primenumbers.net}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 2524190<sup>2097152</sup> + 1 is an 13,426,224-digit [[generalized Fermat prime]], and the largest known non-Mersenne prime {{As of|2025|10|lc=on}}.<ref name="largestprime" />
* ''Mathematics:'' 2<sup>136,279,841</sup> − 1 is a 41,024,320-digit [[Mersenne prime]]; the [[largest known prime]] of any kind {{as of|2025|lc=on}}.<ref name="largestprime">Chris Caldwell, [http://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=3 The Top Twenty: Largest Known Primes] at The [[Prime Pages]].</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' 2<sup>136,279,840</sup> × (2<sup>136,279,841</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1) is an 82,048,640-digit [[perfect number]], the largest known as of 2025.<ref name="mersenneprime">Chris Caldwell, [http://primes.utm.edu/mersenne/index.html Mersenne Primes: History, Theorems and Lists] at The [[Prime Pages]].</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' ''G''(4) = 3 × 2<sup>(3 × 2<sup>27</sup> + 27)</sup> − 2 ≈ {{val|6.895081e121210694}} is the length of the [[Goodstein sequence]] beginning with 4. Its first and last 20 digits are 68950808030926201657...23844928197722374142.<ref>{{cite OEIS|A056193}}</ref>
* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– History:'' 10<sup>8×10<sup>16</sup></sup>, largest named number in [[Archimedes]]' ''[[The Sand Reckoner|Sand Reckoner]]''.
* ''Mathematics:'' The first instance of a 5 in Gijswijt's sequence occurs near index {{val|3.2719044223289929745e125857689874791897769333}} ≈ 10<sup>{{val|1.258577e23}}</sup>.<ref name=gijswijt/>
* ''Mathematics:'' [[Friedman's SSCG function|SSCG(2)]] = 3 × 2<sup>(3 × 2<sup>95</sup>)</sup> − 8 ≈ {{val|3.241704e35775080127201286522908640065}} ≈ 10<sup>{{val|3.577508e28}}</sup>. Its first and last 20 digits are 32417042291246009846...34057047399148290040.
* ''Mathematics:'' 10<sup>googol</sup> (<math>10^{10^{100}}</math>), a [[googolplex]]. A number 1 followed by 1 googol zeros. [[Carl Sagan]] has estimated that 1 googolplex, fully written out, would not fit in the [[observable universe]] because of its size.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0lFQOmb6mVs |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211212/0lFQOmb6mVs| archive-date=2021-12-12 |url-status=live|title=Googol and Googolplex by Carl Sagan|last=asantos|date=15 December 2007|via=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

==Larger than 10<sup>10<sup>100</sup></sup>==
(One [[googolplex]]; 10<sup>googol</sup>; [[Long and short scales|short scale]] and [[long and short scales|long scale]]: googolplex)
* ''Go:'' There are at least 10<sup>10<sup>108</sup></sup> legal games of Go.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Walraet |first1=Matthieu |last2=Tromp |first2=John |title=A Googolplex of Go Games |journal=Computers and Games |date=2016 |volume=10068 |pages=191–201 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-50935-8_18}}</ref>
* ''Go:'' There are at most 10<sup>10<sup>171</sup></sup> legal games of Go.<ref name="Tromp and Farnebäck 2007"/>
* ''Mathematics&nbsp;– Literature:'' The number of different ways in which the books in [[Jorge Luis Borges]]' [[The Library of Babel|Library of Babel]] can be arranged is approximately <math>10^{10^{1\,834\,102}}</math>, the [[factorial]] of the number of books in the Library of Babel.
* ''Mathematics:'' ''F''<sub>18233954</sub> = <math>2^{2^{18\,233\,954}} + 1 \approx 10^{3.733937 \times 10^{5\,488\,966}}</math> is the largest known composite [[Fermat number]] as of 2025.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fermat factoring status |url=http://www.prothsearch.com/fermat.html |website=www.prothsearch.com |access-date=21 March 2026}}</ref>
* ''Cosmology:''  In [[Chaotic Inflation theory|chaotic inflation theory]], proposed by physicist [[Andrei Linde]], our [[universe]] is one of many other universes with different [[physical constant]]s that originated as part of our local section of the [[Multiverse#Bubble theory|multiverse]], owing to a [[vacuum]] that had not decayed to its [[ground state]]. According to Linde and Vanchurin, the total number of these universes is about <math>10^{10^{10\,000\,000}}</math>.<ref>Zyga, Lisa [http://www.physorg.com/news174921612.html "Physicists Calculate Number of Parallel Universes"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110606094329/http://www.physorg.com/news174921612.html |date=2011-06-06 }}, ''[[PhysOrg]]'', 16 October 2009.</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' <math>10^{\,\!10^{10^{34}}}</math>, order of magnitude of an upper bound that occurred in a [[Skewes' number|proof of Skewes]] (this was later estimated to be closer to 1.397 × 10<sup>316</sup>).
* ''Mathematics:'' <math>2^{2^{1729^{12}}} \approx 10^{10^{10^{38.332150}}}</math> is the smallest factor for which the [[multiplication algorithm]] of Harvey and van der Hoeven (2019)<ref name="Harvey-vdHoeven">{{cite journal | last1 = Harvey | first1 = David | last2 = van der Hoeven | first2 = Joris | author2-link = Joris van der Hoeven | doi = 10.4007/annals.2021.193.2.4 | issue = 2 | journal = [[Annals of Mathematics]] | mr = 4224716 | pages = 563–617 | series = Second Series | title = Integer multiplication in time <math>O(n \log n)</math> | volume = 193 | year = 2021| s2cid = 109934776 | url = https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-02070778v2/file/nlogn.pdf }}</ref> is faster than the [[Schönhage–Strassen algorithm]].
* ''Cosmology:'' The estimated number of [[Planck time|Planck time units]] for [[quantum fluctuations]] and [[quantum tunnelling|tunnelling]] to generate a new [[Big Bang]] is estimated to be <math>10^{10^{10^{56}}}</math>.
* ''Mathematics:'' <math>10^{\,\!10^{10^{100}}}</math>, a number in [[Names of large numbers#The googol family|the googol family]] called a googolplexplex, googolplexian, or googolduplex. 1 followed by a googolplex zeros, or 10<sup>googolplex</sup>
* ''Cosmology:'' The uppermost estimate to the size of the entire universe is approximately <math>10^{10^{10^{122}}}</math> times that of the [[observable universe]].<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Susskind's challenge to the Hartle–Hawking no-boundary proposal and possible resolutions |author=Don N. Page for Cornell University |journal= Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics |year=2007 |volume=2007 |issue=1 |page=004 |doi=10.1088/1475-7516/2007/01/004 |arxiv=hep-th/0610199 |bibcode=2007JCAP...01..004P |s2cid=17403084 }}</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' <math>10^{\,\!10^{10^{963}}}</math>, order of magnitude of another upper bound in a proof of [[Stanley Skewes|Skewes]].
* ''Mathematics:'' <math>10^{\,\!10^{10^{10^{100}}}}</math>, a googoltriplex, googolplexianth, or googolplexplexplex, one followed by googolplexplex zeroes.
* ''Mathematics:'' <math>{10 \uparrow \uparrow 100}</math>, a number called giggol, which is 10 [[Tetration|tetrated]] to 100.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Infinity Scrapers |url=http://www.polytope.net/hedrondude/scrapers.htm |access-date=2025-12-07 |website=www.polytope.net}}</ref> It was coined by modifying the vowel sound of "googol".
* ''Mathematics:'' Steinhaus' [[Steinhaus–Moser notation#Mega|mega]] lies between <math>10\uparrow\uparrow257</math> and <math>10\uparrow\uparrow258</math>.
* ''Mathematics:'' ''g''<sub>1</sub> = <math>3\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 3</math>, called a grahal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Forcal - Aarex's Large Numbers |url=https://sites.google.com/site/aarexnumbers/forcal |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160411040939/https://sites.google.com/site/aarexnumbers/forcal |archive-date=2016-04-11 |access-date=2025-12-07 |website=sites.google.com}}</ref> See [[Graham's number]].
* ''Mathematics:'' Moser's number, "2 in a mega-gon" in [[Steinhaus–Moser notation]], is approximately equal to <math>10 \uparrow^{10 \uparrow\uparrow 257} 10</math>; its last four digits are ...1056.
* ''Mathematics:'' [[Graham's number]], defined as ''g''<sub>64</sub> where ''g''<sub>1</sub> is as above and ''g''<sub>''n''</sub> = <math>3 \uparrow^{g_{n-1}} 3</math>. The last ten digits are ...2464195387, and it arises as an upper bound solution to a problem in [[Ramsey theory]].
* ''Mathematics:'' [[Kruskal's tree theorem|TREE(3)]]: appears in relation to a theorem on trees in [[graph theory]].  Representation of the number is difficult, but one weak lower bound is  ''A''<sup>''A''(187196)</sup>(1), where A(n) is a version of the [[Ackermann function]].
* ''Mathematics:'' [[Friedman's SSCG function|SSCG(3)]]: appears in relation to the [[Robertson–Seymour theorem]].  Known to be greater than TREE(3).
* ''Mathematics:'' Transcendental integer: a set of numbers defined in 2000 by [[Harvey Friedman (mathematician)|Harvey Friedman]], appears in proof theory.<ref>H. Friedman, [https://cpb-us-w2.wpmucdn.com/u.osu.edu/dist/1/1952/files/2014/01/EnormousInt.12pt.6_1_00-23kmig3.pdf Enormous integers in real life] (accessed 2021-02-06)</ref>
* ''Mathematics:'' [[Rayo's number]] is a large number named after Agustín Rayo which has been claimed to be the largest number to have ever been named.<ref>{{cite web|title=CH. Rayo's Number|url=http://mathfactor.uark.edu/2007/04/ch-rayos-number/|publisher=The Math Factor Podcast|access-date=24 March 2014}}</ref> It was originally defined in a "big number duel" at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] on 26 January 2007.<ref>{{cite web|last=Kerr|first=Josh|title=Name the biggest number contest|url=http://joshkerr.com/who-can-name-the-bigger-number-contest/|access-date=27 March 2014|date=7 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320033110/http://www.joshkerr.com/who-can-name-the-bigger-number-contest/|archive-date=20 March 2016}}</ref>
